claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin iron-oxide surface film.
The native oxide film on Q235 steel consists primarily of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
The native oxide film acts as a protective barrier for Q235 steel at room temperature.
Limited atomic mobility at room temperature preserves the continuity and adhesion of the native oxide film.
A continuous native oxide film blocks corrosive species from reaching the steel.
Exposure at 700–900 °C accelerates restructuring and cracking of the native oxide film.
High-temperature exposure increases ionic diffusion in the oxide-film system.
High-temperature exposure can induce phase changes or stresses within the native oxide film.
Aggressive salt species destabilize the native oxide film at high temperature.
Salt interaction with the oxide can cause spallation or formation of non-protective corrosion products.
Loss of oxide-film integrity permits accelerated corrosion of Q235 steel.
Room-temperature salt exposure will produce minimal mass change and stable oxide characteristics.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce oxide-film cracking or spallation.
High-temperature salt exposure will increase mass loss relative to room-temperature salt exposure and high-temperature salt-free exposure.
High-temperature salt exposure will form secondary corrosion products that are less protective than the native oxide.
The proposed mechanism applies when uncoated, pre-exposure Q235 steel relies on its native oxide as the sole barrier.
Corrosion-resistant coatings or surface treatments may prevent the proposed mechanism from applying.
A substantially different salt composition may change whether the proposed mechanism applies.
